strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and interesting gap in machine unlearning evaluation: high unlearning accuracy (UA) does not imply the model has removed the influence of forget data, because the true label can remain a plausible candidate. The conformal-prediction analysis in Section 2.2 (Table 3: 30-90% of misclassified forget instances remain in the prediction set) provides concrete evidence for this point.

The proposed metrics (CR, MIACR) are simple, easy to compute from any black-box model, and are supported by an unusually broad empirical study: 9 unlearning methods, two datasets (CIFAR-10, Tiny ImageNet), two architectures (ResNet-18, ViT), random and class-wise forgetting, and multiple alpha values, with variance across 3 trials reported in the appendix.

The paper is honest about a key technical caveat: exchangeability underlying conformal prediction does not hold in unlearning settings (footnote 1), and it additionally analyzes distribution shifts between calibration and forget data (Appendix B.4, shadow/semi-shadow models), showing awareness of the metric's fragility.

The proposed unlearning framework is general and plugs into existing training-based methods (RT, FT, RL), and the ablation in Figures 3-4 (shift of non-conformity score distributions) gives a qualitative sanity check.
weaknesses: Metric validity is not convincingly established. CR = Coverage / Set Size is an ad hoc ratio with no theoretical justification, and it behaves inconsistently: under the gap-to-RT criterion, RL is claimed to outperform methods closer to RT on some comparisons, and Set Size below 1 / empty prediction sets at larger alpha (Section 4.2) show the metric can misrepresent model performance. The paper recommends alpha=0.1 largely empirically rather than principled.

There is circularity between the evaluation metric and the proposed method. The unlearning loss (Eq. 8) directly optimizes the conformal non-conformity score toward the calibrated threshold, i.e., it optimizes the very quantities the CR/MIACR metrics measure. Improvement in CR_Df under this loss is therefore expected by construction and does not independently demonstrate improved 'forgetting.' Missing ablation: a plain margin/C&W-style loss without the conformal threshold (Eq. 7 alone) to isolate the benefit of the conformal component.

The connection between excluding the true label from the prediction set and 'true forgetting' is asserted rather than proven. Reducing confidence in the true label is precisely what many existing unlearning/confidence-reduction losses already do (e.g., confidence penalty, negative-log-likelihood maximization, GA-type methods); the paper does not compare against such simpler loss baselines, making the novelty of the framework modest.

Optimizing the framework moves methods away from the retrain (RT) gold standard rather than toward it: for example, applying the framework to RT raises UA from 8.6% to 14-17.7% (Table 7), which on a gap-to-RT reading worsens unlearning fidelity. The paper acknowledges this only partially.

Only 3 independent trials are used, and several variance estimates are very large (e.g., RL set size std > 16 in Table 12; coverage stds up to 0.5), so some conclusions about method ranking under CR/MIACR may not be statistically robust. No significance testing.

Presentation weaknesses reduce readability: dense and confusing table layouts (UA/RA/TA embedded in method-name rows spanning alpha blocks), typos ('CIFAT-10', 'In addiction'), and notation like z_t(x) introduced but not used in Eq. 7. No code release is mentioned, limiting reproducibility despite detailed hyperparameters.

Related work on conformal prediction-based evaluation of unlearning (Becker & Liebig, 2022) is discussed only briefly; a more direct empirical comparison with that approach, or with other uncertainty-aware unlearning evaluations, is absent.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important question: whether standard unlearning metrics (UA, MIA) actually capture forgetting, and the observation that misclassified forget points often remain in prediction sets is an interesting empirical phenomenon.

The empirical scope is broad: 9 unlearning methods, two datasets (CIFAR-10/ResNet-18, Tiny ImageNet/ViT), random and class-wise forgetting scenarios, multiple α values, 3 seeds with standard deviations in the appendix.

The work is transparent about its assumptions: the footnote acknowledging that exchangeability may not hold in unlearning settings, the analysis of α sensitivity and empty prediction sets (Section 2.4/4.2), and the shadow-model analysis of distribution shift in Appendix B.4 show care.
Implementation details (training recipe, calibration sizes, hyperparameter ranges) are reported thoroughly enough to support reproducibility.
weaknesses: The central validity problem: the retrained (RT) model — the universally accepted gold standard for unlearning — itself shows high in-set ratios and high CR on forget data (e.g., coverage 0.881 and in-set ratios of 30–57% in Tables 3 and 4). This means the proposed metrics flag the ideal outcome as 'not truly forgotten,' suggesting the metrics largely measure generic label predictability of in-distribution images rather than residual model memorization. The paper does not resolve this tension; criterion ➊ (gap to RT) partially concedes the point, while criterion ➊➋ (lower CR on Df is better) contradicts the retraining gold standard and rewards methods like FF that catastrophically destroy utility.

Evaluating conformal coverage on training/forget data lacks the statistical guarantees that motivate conformal prediction (the authors' own footnote admits exchangeability fails), so CR and MIACR are effectively heuristic ratios of softmax confidences; the claimed connection to rigorous uncertainty quantification is overstated, and no theoretical analysis of what these metrics actually measure (or what they guarantee) is provided.

The proposed framework is close to existing confidence-degradation unlearning (gradient ascent/margin-style losses) with the C&W margin replaced by a threshold q̄; with Δ = 0.01 the margin is nearly vacuous. More importantly, the method directly optimizes the proposed metric, creating an evaluation circularity: improved CR_Df under L_unlearn demonstrates the loss does what it is designed to do, not that true forgetting improves. No MIA, retrain-comparison at equal utility budget, or information-theoretic forgetting verification substantiates improved forgetting.

Some conclusions rest on thin or confusing evidence: the MIA-conformal analysis (three prediction sets {0},{1},{0,1}) is poorly motivated and hard to interpret; Grad-CAM claims (Table 1) are anecdotal with a single example; the report that 'the FT method achieves an average gap of 1.47... compared to 2.2' describes a metric where lower UA (worse predictive performance) counts as improvement, which is at odds with how unlearning quality is normally assessed.

The claim that 'many existing methods do not achieve satisfactory forgetting' conflates the behavior of the proposed metric with genuine retained data influence; since RT exhibits the same signatures, the paper's headline negative finding about existing methods is not convincingly established.

Presentation quality is below the bar in places: typos ('In addiction', 'possibility' for 'probability', 'CIFAT-10', 'ReNet18'), Table 1 is an image figure labeled as a table, UA/RA/TA values embedded inside method rows of large tables hurt readability, and Golatkar et al. citation years are inconsistently used (FF attributed to 2020a while the contribution list cites 2020b).
No code release is mentioned, and given the metric-centric contribution, releasing an evaluation toolkit would be important for others to build on the work.

strengths: The core observation is interesting and well-motivated: misclassifying forget data (high UA or successful MIA) does not necessarily mean the model has forgotten it, since the true label may still fall within the conformal prediction set. The Grad-CAM visualization (Table 1) is a compelling qualitative illustration.
The paper connects two active areas—conformal prediction and machine unlearning—in a way that appears largely unexplored, and the metrics CR/MIACR are simple and easy to compute.

The empirical scope is broad: 9 unlearning methods across CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, random and class-wise forgetting, 10%/50% forget ratios, multiple alpha values, 3 random trials with standard deviations, plus a distribution-shift analysis (shadow/semi-shadow models, Appendix B.4).
The proposed unlearning framework is method-agnostic (plugs into RT/FT/RL) and the results show reduced CR_Df with relatively stable retain/test accuracy.
The authors are candid about a key theoretical limitation, noting in a footnote that exchangeability required by conformal prediction may not hold in unlearning settings.
weaknesses: Metric validity is under-argued. The Retrain (RT) model is the accepted gold standard for unlearning, yet criterion (2) ('lower CR of D_f is better') rewards models whose CR_Df falls *below* RT's—for example, FF achieves the lowest CR (0.131 vs RT's 0.943) purely by destroying the model (RA/TA drop to ~40%). A metric that scores a broken model as having the 'best forgetting quality' is not clearly measuring true forgetting, and the tension between criterion (1) (match RT) and criterion (2) (minimize/maximize limits) is never resolved.

The CR definition (Coverage / Set Size) is ad hoc. No justification is given for the specific ratio form, its units/interpretation are opaque, and its behavior can be dominated by set-size anomalies (e.g., set sizes near zero or very large for degenerate models). Alternative aggregations are not ablated.

There is an internal inconsistency in how UA is treated. The central thesis is that high UA does not imply forgetting; yet in Section 4.3, 'significant improvement in UA across all methods' is presented as evidence that the framework improves forgetting quality, and the gap-to-RT criterion relies on moving UA toward RT. The paper does not reconcile why UA is a flawed metric for evaluation but a meaningful signal of success for its own framework.

The paper's headline motivating statistic (54.6% of misclassified forget points remain in-set) lacks a rigorous baseline: no ground-truth measure of information retention (e.g., reconstruction/gradient leakage attacks, retrain-with-noise references, or provable removal bounds) is used to validate that exclusion from the prediction set actually corresponds to data removal. The link between prediction-set membership and 'forgetting' remains heuristic.

The exchangeability/distribution-shift problem is acknowledged but only partially addressed: calibration data is drawn from the test distribution while forget data are training points, so the conformal threshold q is computed on a mismatched distribution. The shadow/semi-shadow remedy appears only in the appendix and is tailored to a single method (RL), and its implications for the main results are not quantified.

The proposed loss (Eq. 8) is essentially a margin loss pushing the non-conformity score of forget data above a calibrated threshold. There is no ablation isolating the contribution of the conformal-calibration term versus a plain C&W or gradient-ascent margin loss with a fixed threshold, so the claim that conformal prediction *as such* improves the unlearning framework is not supported.

MIACR offers limited insight: conformal prediction over a binary MIA outcome yields only sets {0}, {1}, {0,1}, so the metric largely re-encodes MIA behavior with a confidence threshold rather than adding a new uncertainty dimension.

Presentation has multiple defects that impede readability: typos ('CIFAT-10', 'Tabel 4', 'ReNet18', 'In addiction', 'λ ∈ [0, 0.2, 0.5, 0.1]' in Appendix C vs '[0, 0.2, 0.5, 1]' in Section 4.1), inconsistent criteria descriptions, undefined notation (z_t(x) referenced in Eq. 7 explanation but never defined), and very dense tables whose formatting makes the reported 'gap to RT' values hard to verify.

No code release is mentioned, and several choices (Δ = 0.01, λ grid, the 2,000-point calibration budget) would need the code to be faithfully reproduced. Reproducibility is adequate on paper but not demonstrated.

The empirical support for the framework is confined to two image datasets and three base methods; no evaluation on harder forgetting regimes (e.g., noisy forget labels, larger models, LLMs) or against stronger recent unlearning baselines is provided.

strengths: Novel and interesting perspective: applying conformal prediction to diagnose 'fake unlearning' in existing metrics (UA, MIA) is a fresh angle, and the empirical finding that >50% (UA) and ~55% (MIA) of 'forgotten' misclassified points still fall in the prediction set is a concrete, quantified critique of current evaluation practice.

Two new metrics (CR, MIACR) are clearly defined and simple to compute, and the paper provides sensible discussion of hyperparameter choices (confidence level alpha, calibration set size) with stability analysis.

Broad empirical study: 9 unlearning methods across CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, random and class-wise forgetting, multiple alpha values, and ablations (shadow/semi-shadow models for distribution shift; accuracy-vs-epoch curves) give reasonable coverage of the design space.

The proposed CPU framework is simple and general, plugging into existing training-based unlearning methods with a single loss term, and the reported trade-offs (forgetting quality up while RA/TA and CR_{D_test} remain stable) are documented in detail.
Honest limitations discussion (image-classification-only scope, calibration data requirement) and an impact statement are included.
weaknesses: Weak theoretical grounding for the core device: split conformal prediction's coverage guarantee relies on exchangeability between calibration and forget data, but after unlearning the forget data distribution is deliberately shifted (the paper itself shows this discrepancy in Fig. 4a and patches it with heuristic shadow models in Appendix B.5). The paper never clarifies what, if any, guarantee CR/MIACR inherit, leaving the metrics as heuristic ratios rather than principled uncertainty measures.

Potential metric–objective circularity (Goodhart risk): the paper proposes CR/MIACR as the evaluation standard and then optimizes a loss explicitly designed to improve those same quantities, then reports the improvement as evidence of success. Independent validation of genuine forgetting (e.g., stronger/adaptive attacks, retraining-free audits, downstream leakage) is limited to standard UA/MIA, weakening the central claim that CPU achieves more reliable forgetting.

Limited novelty of the learning component: the L_unlearn loss (Eq. 9) essentially reduces to a margin loss pushing the softmax probability of the true label below a calibrated threshold (1 - q_hat + Delta). This is a fairly incremental variation of existing confidence-degradation objectives (NegGrad+, RL, gradient ascent), with the threshold being the main new element; framing it via C&W is more motivational than substantive.

The MIACR construction is under-specified: applying conformal prediction to the binary MIA output space {0,1} requires its own calibration procedure for membership scores, but the paper does not explain how the non-conformity score and calibration are set up in that space, making the metric hard to reproduce or interpret.

CR as Coverage/Set Size has stability issues that are not analyzed: as Set Size approaches zero (which the appendix notes happens, producing empty sets at alpha=0.2), CR can become ill-behaved or gameable, e.g., by a method collapsing to near-uniform or very low-confidence predictions; sensitivity of method rankings to alpha is acknowledged but not resolved.

Presentation flaws: the research-question numbering jumps from Q2 to Q4 (Q3 is missing), several tables (e.g., Tables 9, 12, 14) are dense to the point of illegibility, and some claims (e.g., 'improves the UA of existing unlearning methods by an average of 6.6%') mix metric improvement with method improvement in a potentially misleading way. No code release is mentioned, which hurts reproducibility of the exact thresholds and calibration splits.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely underexplored question: whether common unlearning metrics (UA, MIA) truly certify forgetting, and it brings an uncertainty-quantification lens (conformal prediction) to unlearning evaluation, which is a fresh angle.

The experimental scope is reasonably broad for the evaluation part: 9 unlearning methods across CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, with random and class-wise forgetting, sensitivity analysis over alpha and calibration size, and ablations in the appendix.

The proposed CPU framework is simple and general: it wraps existing training-based unlearning methods with an extra C&W-inspired loss term, and the reported retain/test accuracy degradation is small, which is practically appealing.

The appendix honestly examines distribution shift between calibration and forget data (Figure 4) and proposes shadow/semi-shadow mitigations, and the limitations section (Appendix D) candidly discusses task scope and calibration-data assumptions.
weaknesses: Central conceptual flaw: the 'fake unlearning' evidence does not distinguish memorization from valid coverage. Split conformal prediction guarantees the true label lies in the set for ~95% of any exchangeable data, so a high 'recover/in-set' ratio on forget data is exactly what valid conformal prediction predicts for data the model has genuinely forgotten. The correct analysis is a differential comparison of coverage on forget data versus held-out test/calibration data, which the paper has (Table 3) but does not use to support the Section 2.2 claim. By the paper's own logic, even Retrain — the gold standard — shows 30-57% in-set ratios (Table 2/6), i.e., massive 'fake unlearning' under perfect retraining, which the authors never confront. This undercuts the paper's headline finding.

The proposed metrics are ad hoc and partly circular. CR (Coverage/Set Size) has no theoretical justification and discards conformal validity; MIACR merely checks that the prediction set equals {0}, which reduces to a confidence-thresholding rule dressed in conformal terminology. The 'superiority' validation (Figures 7-10: CR-identified forgotten points have lower softmax / higher loss than UA-identified ones) is essentially true by construction, since CR-identified points are precisely those with high non-conformity scores.

The unlearning framework optimizes the proposed metric directly (pushing true-label non-conformity above q_hat), so improvements in CR/UA are expected by construction; the claimed '6.6% average UA improvement' is largely a restatement of the training objective rather than independent evidence of better forgetting.

MIACR behaves counter-intuitively as a forgetting measure: the Retrain baseline achieves a very low MIACR (e.g., 0.018-0.039) while supposedly weaker methods score higher, suggesting the metric does not track 'good unlearning' in the way claimed. This anomaly is reported but not explained or reconciled.

The evaluation is confined to image classification with two architectures and two datasets; no language/generative settings, no comparison to alternative reliability baselines (e.g., calibration/ECE-based or influence-based forgetting measures), limiting the claimed generality of the 'redefined' unlearning evaluation.

The method's practicality depends on exchangeability between calibration and forget data, which the authors themselves show is violated for label-corruption methods (Appendix B.5), requiring additional shadow-model training — adding notable overhead and complexity that is not reflected in the main-text framework.

Presentation issues: research question Q3 is skipped (numbering jumps from Q2 to Q4), Figure 1 is hard to parse without extensive caption study, several typos remain (e.g., 'In addition' in the conclusion), and Table 3 is very dense. No code release is mentioned, weakening reproducibility for a metrics/benchmark-style contribution.

strengths: The paper identifies a genuine and under-explored gap in machine unlearning evaluation: point-prediction metrics (UA, MIA) do not capture residual information about forget data visible through the model's uncertainty. The 'fake unlearning' observation is a useful reframing of how forgetting quality should be audited.

The proposed metrics (CR, MIACR) are simple, model-agnostic, and easy to compute, and the paper is careful about practical details: choice of confidence level alpha, stability of the conformal quantile with calibration set size (Figure 2), and sensitivity analyses over alpha in the appendix.

The evaluation is broad: 9-10 unlearning methods across CIFAR-10/ResNet-18 and Tiny ImageNet/ViT, both random and class-wise forgetting scenarios, 3 trials with standard deviations, and multiple evaluation scenarios in a substantial appendix (Tables 6-14).

The proposed CPU framework is a lightweight, general add-on (a single conformally thresholded C&W-style loss term) that improves UA and CR on forget data across methods while keeping retain/test accuracy and CR on test data approximately stable (Tables 5, 14), and the ablation with non-conformity score distributions (Figures 5-6) supports the mechanism.

The appendix honestly addresses a distribution-shift concern (label-corruption methods like RL/Salun make forget data non-exchangeable with calibration data) and proposes semi-shadow/shadow model corrections, and the limitations section is candid about the image-classification-only scope and calibration data requirements.
weaknesses: The central 'fake unlearning' claim needs a more careful statistical treatment. Split conformal prediction guarantees marginal coverage of roughly 1-alpha for data exchangeable with the calibration set. Therefore observing that the true label of many misclassified forget points lies in the prediction set is, to a substantial degree, expected behavior of a valid conformal procedure rather than direct evidence of information retention. The paper never analyzes its observed in-set ratios (30-90%) against the nominal 95% coverage or against a null/exchangeability baseline, so it is unclear how much of the effect is a CP artifact versus genuine memorization.

Metric validity is undermined by the behavior on the gold standard: even Retrain (RT), which is by definition complete unlearning, shows high in-set ratios (e.g., 57.3% and 53.2% in Table 2 for MIA) and non-trivial CR_Df values in Tables 3 and 7-12. A metric under which the ground-truth upper bound performs this poorly is arguably miscalibrated, and the paper does not discuss or justify this. The 'gap to RT' criterion then measures distance to a reference that itself fails the proposed criterion.

CR (Coverage/Set Size) is ad hoc: there is no theoretical or empirical analysis of its behavior under known memorization levels (e.g., synthetic data poisoning with controlled canary strength), no comparison against stronger existing unlearning audits (e.g., exact retrain divergence, influence-function estimates, or membership-inference audits with proper calibration), and the choice to divide by Set Size is not justified beyond intuition. The claimed 'superiority' of the metrics is largely asserted from ranking shifts rather than validated against an external ground truth of what the model actually retained.

The MIACR definition is conceptually opaque: it applies conformal prediction to membership labels {0,1} produced by an MIA attack, so the metric inherits all weaknesses of the underlying MIA (threshold choice, attack strength) and is sensitive to that pipeline; error bars and sensitivity of MIACR to the MIA configuration are not reported.

The CPU framework's practical significance is limited: for methods already near RT (e.g., Salun, SFRon), the improvement is small, and the reported '6.6% average UA improvement' is driven substantially by weaker baselines; additionally the framework requires held-out calibration data and (for label-corruption methods) training shadow/semi-shadow models, whose cost and effect on the coverage guarantee are not formally analyzed (the exchangeability assumption underlying the CP guarantee is broken by the unlearning procedure itself, and only empirically patched in Appendix B.5).

Scope is narrow: only image classification on CIFAR-10 and Tiny ImageNet, two model architectures, and small-scale forgetting fractions; no LLM or generative-model experiments despite privacy being the motivating scenario. No code release is mentioned, which weakens reproducibility for a paper whose contribution is primarily evaluation infrastructure.

Presentation issues: several tables are dense and hard to parse (Tables 7-13 compress six quantities per row), notation such as q-hat subscripts is inconsistent, there are typographical errors (e.g., 'In addiction' in the conclusion), and some claims in the abstract/introduction ('significantly push the ground truth label out of the set', 'improves the UA of existing unlearning methods by an average of 6.6%') are stated more strongly than the evidence supports.
